name: Placenta / sheep placenta creams

image.caption: Twee metalen tubes, “Neo Placenta Neo Vita” in de originele verpakking met bijsluiter, kapper Van Vliet, objectnr 84669-A-E

lead: Placenta creams contain extract from sheep or other animal placenta and are sold as anti-aging moisturisers. The payoff people want is smoother, better-hydrated skin with softer-looking lines.

Makers say the extract supplies amino acids, peptides, vitamins and growth factors such as EGF and IGF-1 that support skin regeneration. Extracts are made by enzymatic hydrolysis and purification. Wikipedia notes some cultures use placenta in cosmetics without assessing efficacy, and no clinical studies of appearance outcomes were found in the sources reviewed.

paras: People use them as a moisturiser or treatment step in a daily skincare routine, applied to the face and neck, often alongside sunscreen and a regular cleanser. They are sold over the counter as cosmetics, and users generally judge results over several weeks of consistent use.

Safety data were not found in the sources reviewed. Products are generally sold as cosmetics rather than drugs, so ingredient quality and concentration vary by brand. As with any new topical, irritation or allergic reaction is possible, and people with sensitive skin or known animal-product allergies may want to patch test first.

angle.text: Sheep placenta creams are used as an anti-aging step for smoother, more moisturised skin and fewer visible wrinkles. The idea is that the extract's peptides and growth-type signals nudge skin cells toward renewal. No clinical studies of the appearance claims were found.

lead: Placenta creams are topical skincare products containing extracts of animal placenta, most often sheep, and also horse, pig or cattle. They are used on the face, usually at night, with the aim of firmer, smoother, better-hydrated skin and softer fine lines.[1][2]

The extracts are made by enzymatic breakdown and purification, and makers describe them as containing amino acids, peptides, vitamins and growth factors such as EGF, IGF-1 and TGF-beta, which is the basis of the anti-ageing and skin-regeneration pitch.[1] Wikipedia notes that placenta has also been used in cosmetics, pharmaceuticals and traditional medicine in several cultures.

Published human research is small. A 2023 randomized single-blind half-face study of a horse-placenta eye cream in 24 Japanese women reported a small improvement in eye-corner wrinkle grade after two weeks; the authors were employees of the manufacturer and noted the lack of a placebo group.[2]
infobox: Nightly, targeted at adults over 30 (as marketed)
Generally sold as cosmetics in the US and EU; EU bans human-derived placenta ingredients (per Grokipedia)

paras: Sheep placenta from New Zealand and Australia is described as the most common source, with equine, porcine and bovine placenta as alternatives.[1] Extraction typically uses enzymes to break the tissue into peptides, followed by purification and freeze-drying, and formulations combine the extract with emollients, humectants, antioxidants and preservatives.[1]

Grokipedia, an AI-generated reference, reports folk use of placenta for skin, scientific interest in its growth factors in the 1930s and 1940s, a French cream called Placentor around 1959 and a placenta cosmetic launched in the US in 1958, with commercial growth from the 1970s and later markets in Japan, Australia, New Zealand and Korea.[1] These details are unverified against primary sources.
Wikipedia notes that dried placenta (ziheche) is used in traditional Chinese medicine, and that placentophagy is a recent practice in some Western cultures.

A 2023 randomized, single-blind, half-face study in Japan applied a horse-placenta-based eye cream twice daily for two weeks to one side of the face in 24 women with mild to moderate eye-corner wrinkles. Expert grading fell from 2.25 to 2.0 on the treated side while the untreated side stayed at 2.0, and skin-replica analysis showed significant reductions in maximum wrinkle width and wrinkle count but not in depth or area. No adverse events were reported. The authors, employees of the manufacturer, noted the absence of a placebo group, the short duration and the small sample.[2]

Grokipedia states that evidence generally consists of small, short trials of 20 to 50 participants over 2 to 4 weeks, and that researchers call for larger, longer studies.[1] An oral porcine placenta extract trial in a different category (a supplement taken by mouth) has reported effects on skin hydration and wrinkles and is not evidence for creams.[3]

According to Grokipedia, a 2002 Cosmetic Ingredient Review panel found insufficient data to judge the safety of placental extracts and recommended further study of sensitization and toxicity; allergic reaction to animal proteins, hormone-related concerns during pregnancy, and sourcing and pathogen risks are listed, and patch testing is suggested.[1] It reports the products are generally regulated as cosmetics in the US and EU, that the FDA has an import alert on bovine placenta because of BSE risk, and that the EU bans human-derived placenta ingredients.[1]
